newsitem.title: ANGOLA: U.N. says Angolan army denying it access to areas.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Angolan army denying it access to areas.

text.p: The United Nations peacekeeping mission in Angola on Thursday criticised the Angolan government for denying its observers access to areas in the northeast to verify reports of troop movements.

"The FAA (Angolan Armed Forces) authorities...declined to allow UNAVEM III to verify troop movements...in spite of repeated requests," the U.N. mission (UNAVEM), helping to implement a 1994 peace treaty between the Angolan government and former rebel UNITA, said in a statement.
The government's army has launched an offensive into diamond-rich UNITA areas since May 20 in contravention of the peace agreement.
U.N. military observers were only allowed into the areas where fighting had been reported three weeks later after permission from President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
After visiting the area the U.N. said it could not find proof of heavy battles, but confirmed government troops had moved into 10 border areas previously controlled by UNITA.

The U.N. statement on Thursday said it had again not been allowed to travel in areas of the northeast and had been told by the government the area was unsafe. It pointed out that the government had taken Angolan journalists near the frontlines last week.

"UNAVEM wonders why such expedient access to an alleged battlefield was allowed to these journalists, while only two days before, on June 19, U.N. teamsite observers in nearby Andrada (Nzage) were once again informed that they could not patrol outside the town 'for their own safety'," the statement said.
The U.N. statement also denied accusations by UNITA that it had underplayed the government offensive in the northeast and was favouring the government.
"UNAVEM reported accurately what they have seen in the areas made accessible to them," the statement said.
The world body called on the government to halt all military activity in the northeast and urged UNITA to provide information about its military capabilities.
UNITA declared last year it had disarmed all its troops, but the Angolan government says the movement still has an army of about 35,000.

The government has also accused the former rebels, with whom it has shared a unity government since April, of harbouring soldiers once loyal to former Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko, toppled in May by rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
